items.prompt: What is the name for the process by which one tectonic plate is forced beneath another, often leading to mountain building?

options.label: Folding
options.feedback: Folding bends rock layers, but subduction involves one plate sliding under another — that is the process that builds some mountain ranges.

options.label: Erosion
options.feedback: Erosion wears mountains down; the process that pushes one plate under another is subduction, not erosion.

options.label: Subduction
options.feedback: Correct — subduction is the sinking of one plate beneath another, and it builds volcanic mountain ranges.

options.label: Uplift
options.feedback: Uplift is the rising of land, but it is often a result of subduction, not the name of the plate-against-plate process itself.

items.ok_line: Subduction is the key movement that builds some mountains.
items.ko_line: Remember: subduction is the specific plate movement.
items.exp_text: Subduction is when one tectonic plate slides beneath another into the mantle. It happens at ocean trenches and builds volcanic mountain ranges along the coast.

items.prompt: What are the three main rock types that mountains can be made of?

options.label: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic
options.feedback: Correct — these are the three rock types, and mountains can contain any or all of them.

options.label: Granite, basalt, and limestone
options.feedback: Those are specific rocks, not the three broad categories; igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic are the general types.

options.label: Volcanic, crustal, and mantle
options.feedback: Those are sources of rock, not rock types; the three types are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.

options.label: Old, young, and ancient
options.feedback: Those describe age, not rock type; the types are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.

items.ok_line: The three rock types are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.
items.ko_line: Specific rocks are not the main types.
items.exp_text: Mountains are made from igneous rock (cooled magma), sedimentary rock (layers of sediment), or metamorphic rock (changed by heat and pressure). Any mountain can contain all three.

items.prompt: What is the name of the theory that explains how mountains are formed by the movement of large pieces of Earth's outer shell?

options.label: Plate tectonics
options.feedback: Correct — plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's surface is divided into plates that move and collide, folding and lifting rock to build mountains.

options.label: Continental drift
options.feedback: Continental drift is an older idea about continents moving, but plate tectonics is the full theory that includes the mechanism of plate movement.

options.label: Evolutionary geology
options.feedback: That is not a standard theory for mountain formation; plate tectonics is the accepted explanation.

options.label: Erosion theory
options.feedback: Erosion wears mountains down; it does not explain how they are built. Plate tectonics does.

items.ko_line: Drift is not the full theory.
items.exp_text: Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into rigid plates that move on the softer mantle beneath. Where plates collide, mountains rise.

items.prompt: What kind of mountain forms when molten rock pushes up from below and cools into solid rock, often creating a dome-shaped peak?

options.label: Folded mountain
options.feedback: Folded mountains form when rock layers bend, not from molten rock pushing up; dome mountains come from magma rising.

options.label: Fault-block mountain
options.feedback: Fault-block mountains form when blocks of crust tilt or slide along faults, not from magma pushing up.

options.label: Volcanic mountain
options.feedback: Volcanic mountains are built from lava and ash erupting at the surface, but dome mountains are made by magma that cools beneath the ground and then gets exposed.

options.label: Dome mountain
options.feedback: Correct — a dome mountain forms when magma pushes up the crust into a dome and then cools, often later exposed by erosion.

items.ok_line: Dome mountains come from rising magma.
items.ko_line: This is not folding or faulting.
items.exp_text: A dome mountain forms when a large body of magma pushes up the overlying rock into a rounded dome. After cooling, erosion can expose the hardened rock as a mountain.

items.prompt: Which type of mountain is built primarily from layers of lava and ash piling up from repeated eruptions?

options.label: Dome mountain
options.feedback: Dome mountains come from magma cooling beneath the surface, not from lava and ash piling up; volcanic mountains are built by eruptions.

options.label: Volcanic mountain
options.feedback: Correct — volcanic mountains grow as eruptions deposit layer upon layer of lava and ash.

options.label: Folded mountain
options.feedback: Folded mountains form from rock layers bending, not from volcanic eruptions; volcanic mountains are built by lava and ash.

options.label: Fault-block mountain
options.feedback: Fault-block mountains form from crust moving along faults, not from layered eruptions.

items.ok_line: Volcanoes build mountains from lava and ash.
items.ko_line: This is not a dome or a fold.
items.exp_text: A volcanic mountain grows each time a volcano erupts, depositing lava and ash that harden into new layers. Over time, these layers pile up into a tall cone.

items.prompt: What is the name for the high, rugged part of a mountain range that has been shaped by erosion into sharp peaks and ridges?

options.label: Mountain crest
options.feedback: Correct — the crest is the topmost ridge of a mountain range, often sharp and rocky due to erosion.

options.label: Mountain base
options.feedback: The base is the bottom of the mountain, not the high rugged part; the crest is the top.

options.label: Mountain valley
options.feedback: A valley is a low area between mountains, not a high part.

options.label: Mountain slope
options.feedback: A slope is the inclined side of the mountain, but the crest is the very top ridge.

items.ok_line: The crest is the mountain's top ridge.
items.ko_line: It is not the base or valley.
items.exp_text: The crest of a mountain range is its highest continuous ridge. Erosion carves it into sharp peaks and jagged edges, especially in young mountains.

items.prompt: What is the name for the deep, wide valley carved by a glacier moving through a mountain range?

options.label: V-shaped valley
options.feedback: A V-shaped valley is carved by a river, not a glacier; glaciers carve U-shaped valleys.

options.label: Canyon
options.feedback: A canyon is typically carved by a river, often with steep sides; a glacier-carved valley is U-shaped.

options.label: U-shaped valley
options.feedback: Correct — glaciers carve wide, U-shaped valleys, unlike the narrow V-shapes made by rivers.

options.label: Gorge
options.feedback: A gorge is a narrow, steep-sided valley, not the broad shape formed by a glacier.

items.ko_line: It is not V-shaped or a canyon.
items.exp_text: When a glacier flows down a mountain, it grinds the valley into a wide, flat-bottomed U shape. Rivers cut narrow V shapes, but ice cuts broad U shapes.

items.prompt: What is the name for a fracture in a mountain's rock along which movement has occurred, often creating steep cliffs?

options.label: Fold
options.feedback: A fold is a bend in rock layers, not a fracture; a fault is a break with movement.

options.label: Crevice
options.feedback: A crevice is a narrow crack, but it does not involve movement of the rock on either side; a fault does.

options.label: Erosion surface
options.feedback: Erosion surfaces are worn flat areas, not fractures; a fault is a break.

options.label: Fault
options.feedback: Correct — a fault is a fracture in rock where the two sides have moved past each other, and such movement can build mountains.

items.ok_line: A fault is a fracture with movement.
items.ko_line: It is not a fold or a simple crack.
items.exp_text: A fault is a break in rock where blocks slide past each other. When they heave upward, fault-block mountains form, often with steep cliffs along the fault line.

items.prompt: What is the name for the process by which heavy rock layers squeeze together and shorten, making mountains rise?

options.label: Extension
options.feedback: Extension pulls rock apart, not together; compression squeezes it and builds mountains.

options.label: Compression
options.feedback: Correct — compression is the squeezing of rock layers, which folds and lifts them into mountains.

options.label: Shearing
options.feedback: Shearing pushes rock sideways past each other, not together; compression is the squeezing force.

options.label: Subduction
options.feedback: Subduction is a plate process that can cause compression, but compression itself is the squeezing of rock layers.

items.ok_line: Compression squeezes rock to build mountains.
items.ko_line: It is not extension or shearing.
items.exp_text: Compression pushes rock layers together, making them fold, break, and stack upward. This is how many mountain ranges, especially at colliding plate boundaries, gain height.

items.prompt: What is the name for the highest point of a mountain?

options.label: Summit
options.feedback: Correct — the summit is the very top peak of a mountain.

options.label: Base
options.feedback: The base is the bottom of the mountain, not the top.

options.label: Slope
options.feedback: A slope is the inclined side of the mountain, not its highest point.

options.label: Ridge
options.feedback: A ridge is a long crest, but the summit is the single highest point.

items.ok_line: The summit is the mountain's top.
items.ko_line: It is not the base or slope.
items.exp_text: The summit is the highest point of a mountain. Every mountain has exactly one summit, even if the ridge leading to it has many bumps.
